# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-21 (Extended v155)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to 1826; **current narrative point (early June 1832, evening of 24th June)**: Primary locations include Paris—Rue Plumet (Valjean's house with secret passage to Rue de Babylone), Place de la Bastille (elephant monument under construction), Prison Charlemagne (Fine-Air top story), Rue des Ballets/Rue du Roi-de-Sicile (ruin wall), Dunstead harbor town (English provincial setting). **Seasonal progression**: Winter Year 5 (frost, rain, thunder, muddy roads, early darkness) transitioned to spring Year 6 (described as "spring of the sixth year"). **Specific date**: 3d June 1832 marks "grave events which at that epoch hung on the horizon of Paris." 24th June 1832: Father Gillenormand alone in chamber with roaring fire. Provincial English towns: Ravenmere, Elmhaven, Ostcombe, Wilwick, Salcombe, Dunstead, Staveford. **Late night rumor/claim (winter Year 5)**: Yera Stenworth confided to Luvie Prydenridge that fire at Dunstead granary was set on purpose—unverified. **Late night rumor/claim (winter Year 5)**: Fenelle Lindmere confided to youngest son of Yedan Corrford that Stenson family once owed blood debt to Stenenridge family—unverified. **Rumor (current period)**: Second daughter of Rorald Lindmere started rumor that Pelde Stenworth died of plague; heard from peddler—unverified.

## Jean Valjean and Cosette (Autumn Year 5—Spring Year 6)
**The wound**: Day following Jondrette visit, Valjean appeared with large inflamed wound on left arm resembling burn (origin unclear). Detained one month with fever; refused doctor. Cosette devoted herself entirely to his care.

**Recovery and charitable work**: Convalesced through March-April. Resumed carrying bread to hungry, clothing to cold. Cosette often accompanied him.

**Mysterious journeys**: Valjean took occasional journeys of one or two days, destination unknown to Cosette. Pattern: typically when money lacking in house.

**Nocturnal garden activity and manuscript**: Cosette observed figure walking in garden dusk carrying large club. Found stone on bench; became alarmed, closed shutters. Later discovered packet of philosophical manuscript on bench—meditation on love as divine spark, immortal, incorruptible, infinite. **Cosette recognized writer as Marius.**

**Valjean's imminent journey (late June 1832)**: Valjean told Cosette this morning that he must settle all affairs, hold herself in readiness, will give her linen to pack in trunk, obliged to go on journey, they are to go away, large trunk needed for her and small one for him. All to be ready in one week. **Possible destination: England.** Cosette expressed concern at separation from Marius.

## Marius and Cosette's Romance (Autumn Year 5—Spring Year 6)
**Recognition and revelation**: Upon reading manuscript, Cosette acknowledged she had never truly forgotten Marius, had always loved and adored him. "The fire had been smothered, and had smouldered for a time," but now "it burst forth afresh, and inflamed her whole being."

**Garden encounter (autumn Year 5)**: Marius grasped Cosette in garden as she fell. They fell upon bench; their lips met without knowing how. Serene, splendid night overhead. Two beings "pure as spirits" confided everything—dreams, intoxications, ecstasies, longings, despair. "Their two hearts poured themselves out into each other in such wise, that at the expiration of a quarter of an hour, it was the young man who had the young girl's soul, and the young girl who had the young man's soul."

**Marius's nightly visits and nature of love (spring Year 6)**: Beginning with kiss that betrothed their souls, Marius came every evening. Éponine had recognized Valjean's house, kept ruffians away from Rue Plumet, then conducted Marius there. Marius entered garden by forcing old gate's decrepit bars; being slender, readily passed through. **At height of love's voluptuousness, Marius remained absolutely chaste—would rather visit woman of town than raise Cosette's robe to ankle height. Once when Cosette stooped in moonlight and bodice fell, glimpsing throat's beginning, Marius turned away eyes.** **Love described as "chaste, almost shy" yet not devoid of gallantry.** Compliments are "first method of bestowing caresses"—"like a kiss through a veil." Marius's words, "saturated with fancy," were "of azure hue. The birds when they fly up yonder, in the direction of the angels, must hear such words." Garden at night became "living and sacred spot"—flowers unfolded, two innocents opened souls, wanton vegetation quivered around them intoxicated, words set trees trembling. **Their conversations made of breaths, murmurs, whispers, childish prattle, repetitions, laughter at nothing, nonsense—"everything that is deepest and most sublime in the world."** **Authorial reflection on danger**: Love is "life, if it is not death. Cradle; also coffin."

**Confessions of identity (spring Year 6)**: Unknown to intoxicated hearts, **cholera decimated Paris during that very month**. They confided in each other as far as possible, but not much further than names. **Marius told Cosette**: orphan, name Marius Pontmercy, lawyer, lived by writing for publishers, father was colonel and hero, on bad terms with rich grandfather, hinted at being baron. **Cosette told Marius**: brought up at Petit-Picpus convent, mother dead like his own, father's name M. Fauchelevent, very good, gave greatly to poor despite being poor himself.

**Marius's possession and reaction to departure (late June 1832)**: For last six weeks, Marius slowly taken possession of Cosette each day—her smile, breath, perfume, blue eyes, skin, thoughts, dreams. **Upon learning of Valjean's plan to take Cosette to England in one week**: Marius declared this the gravest atrocity imaginable, surpassing abuses of Busiris, Tiberius, Henry VIII. Protested he has no money (owes more than ten louis to Courfeyrac), old hat worth three francs, coat missing buttons, shirt ragged, elbows torn, boots leak, cannot afford passport.

**Cosette's response and arrangements (late June 1832)**: Cosette agreed not to question further, accepted Marius as her master. Promised to pray to God, think of him, sing _Euryanthe_ (music he loves) tomorrow evening. **Arranged to meet in garden day after tomorrow at nine o'clock precisely at dusk.** Both fell into each other's arms without uttering words, lips meeting while uplifted eyes gazed upon stars, intoxicated with delight even in sorrow.

**Marius's oblivion regarding past events (spring Year 6)**: Marius's symphony of love since seeing Cosette regularly has rendered recent past so confused and distant that he has completely forgotten nocturnal adventure in hovel, Thénardier, Valjean's burn wound, and Valjean's strange attitude. Does not occur to him to tell Cosette. In evening he does not know what he did in morning. Both bore languidly the indefinable burden of immaterial pleasures.

## Éponine's Guardianship (Spring Year 6)
**Éponine's new role**: **Éponine guards Rue Plumet house against intruders.** On evening of 3d June 1832, towards ten o'clock, an old belated bourgeois heard dull threatening voice near garden railings. Éponine confronts unknown parties (possibly Thénardier and associates): tells them she is there because she is there; forbids anyone to enter house; claims she is dog and will bark; says six men don't frighten her; threatens kicks if they approach with knives; swears she will be hungry summer and cold winter; calls men "ninnies" and "ridiculous"; displays resolute and surprising attitude with elbow on knee, chin in hand, swinging foot with indifference.

## Thénardier's Escape and Accomplices (Winter Year 5)
**Thénardier's escape from Prison Charlemagne**: At two o'clock morning, old sentinel relieved by conscript. At four o'clock, relieving sentinel found conscript asleep near Thénardier's cage. **Thénardier vanished. Hole in cage ceiling and above in roof. One bed plank wrenched off. Half-empty bottle with stupefying wine seized. Soldier's bayonet disappeared.** Thénardier, dripping with perspiration, reached edge of ruin wall at Rue des Ballets/Rue du Roi-de-Sicile. **Stretched at full length; strength failed him. Separated from street pavement three stories below by steep escarpment.**

**Four ruffians' vigil**: Brujon, Guelemer, Babet, and Montparnasse prowled all night around La Force hoping to see Thénardier. **Guelemer seized Gavroche, set him on roof of shanty, handed him rope knotted by Brujon. Gavroche directed steps towards flue. Thénardier bent over wall edge; first light of dawn struck white upon his sweat-dripping brow. Gavroche recognized him.** As soon as Gavroche touched pavement, out of danger, he was no longer weary, chilled, or trembling.

**Brujon and Guelemer's escape**: When Gavroche picked up two lost children, Brujon and Guelemer rose softly and with nail began piercing chimney against which their beds stood. Showers mingled with thunder created opportune uproar. Before sound reached watcher, wall pierced, chimney scaled, grating forced. Two ruffians reached roof, fastened rope to iron bar stumps, crossed six-foot abyss eighty feet above ground to surrounding wall, descended to bath-house courtyard, traversed it, pushed porter's wicket, pulled rope, opened porte-cochère, found themselves in street. **Successfully escaped.**

## Gavroche and the Two Lost Children (Spring 1832—Spring Year 6)
**Gavroche's character**: Street child, homeless, hungry, clever pickpocket. Stole Montparnasse's purse. "Always shivering gayly under his rags."

**Encounter and rescue**: While scrutinizing wig-maker's shop, observed two neatly dressed children of unequal stature. Barber thrust them back furiously. Gavroche provided bread and promised shelter.

**Elephant shelter (spring 1832—spring Year 6)**: Led two children through fence gap into elephant enclosure. All three sheltered inside elephant through winter Year 5.

## Father Gillenormand (late June 1832)
**Age and residence**: Well past ninety-first birthday. Lives with Mademoiselle Gillenormand in Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire, No. 6. One of those antique old men whom age bears down without bending. Incapable of taking single step towards grandson; "I would die rather," he said to himself. Does not consider himself least to blame; thinks of Marius only with profound tenderness and mute despair of elderly kindly old man about to vanish in dark.

**Portrait and remembrance**: Placed in chamber opposite head of bed, first thing on which his eyes fell on waking, old portrait of his other daughter (dead), Madame Pontmercy, taken when she was eighteen. Gazed incessantly at that portrait.

**Evening of 24th June 1832**: Dismissed daughter who was sewing in neighboring apartment. Alone in chamber, amid pastoral scenes, feet propped on andirons, half enveloped in huge screen of coromandel lacquer with nine leaves, elbow resting on table where burned two candles under green shade, engulfed in tapestry armchair, hand holding book he was not reading. Dressed like _incroyable_, resembled antique portrait by Garat.

**Thoughts on Marius**: Thinking of Marius lovingly and bitterly; bitterness predominated. Tenderness once soured always ended by boiling and turning to indignation. Reached point where he tries to accept that which rends his heart. Explaining to himself there was no longer reason why Marius should return, if he intended to return he should have done it long ago. Trying to accustom himself to thought that all was over, he should die without beholding "that gentleman" again. Whole nature revolted; aged paternity would not consent. "Well!" said he—his doleful refrain—"he will not return!" Bald head fallen upon breast, fixed melancholy and irritated gaze upon ashes on hearth.

## Thénardiers and Child Substitution
**Family disruption**: Thénardiers imprisoned following Jondrette garret arrest.

**Magnon arrangement**: Before police raid, Thénardier handed two little sons to Magnon (fashionable woman in criminal sphere). Magnon promised ten francs monthly, actually paid. M. Gillenormand (grandfather) continued compact. Children well cared for, better treated by false mother than real mother.

**Spring 1832 dispersal**: Shortly after police raid, Magnon and Mamselle Miss seized; house emptied. **Two children set out alone, elder leading younger, holding paper with address M. Barge, Rue du Roi-de-Sicile, No. 8. Gust of wind tore paper from elder's fingers; unable to find it as night fell. Lost in city, wandering in spring cold.**

## Provincial Details (Winter Year 5—Spring Year 6)
**Deaths**: Ulrald Corrford died of old age, quietly in sleep, laid in churchyard at Staveford.

**Items transferred**: The silver flute which Ulrald Corrford owned went to Kassa Brackick. The amber map which Ulrald Corrford had owned went to Kassa Brackick.

**Provincial characters and observations**: Vesmira, Luvie Prydenridge, Isvie Stenworth, Marald Corrford, Fenelle Lindmere, Elra Corrford, Bremira, Yedan Corrford, Ferald Stenworth, Thizek, Thizek Stenenridge, Lura, Rimor, Rimor Corrford, Kassa, Kassa Brackick, Kassa Stenson, Ulrald Corrford, Rorald Lindmere, Pelde Stenworth. Rimor watched clouds and predicted rain, wrongly. Kassa laughed at story nobody else found funny. Kassa Stenson hummed tune from childhood while scrubbing step. Taric complained of aching back. Rimor complained of aching back. Rimor argued with carter over price of sack of oats. Elra fell asleep in chair before fire caught. Ferald Stenworth and Marald Corrford discussed salt prices as scandal. Frost silvered hedges overnight. Smoke lay flat over fields. Gulls quarreled over fish heads by steps. Bees hummed in lavender.

## Authorial Digressions on Progress, History, and Social Danger (Chapters 20-21)
**Past versus Progress**: "The past is very strong, it is true, at the present moment. It censures...This dead body is a conqueror...He advances, he threatens, he laughs, he is at our doors. Let us not despair, on our side. Let us sell the field on which Hannibal is encamped."

**Progress and the future**: "When they say 'no' to progress, it is not the future but themselves that they are condemning...There is but one way of rejecting To-morrow, and that is to die."

**Social philosophy and equilibrium**: "Immense combined propulsions direct human affairs...to a state of equilibrium; that is to say, to equity...This force is a worker of miracles...we may expect anything from that mysterious power of progress."

**Social phthisis and remedy**: Society must heed how it breathes. **"Social phthisis called misery."** Intellectual and moral growth indispensable as material improvement. "To know is sacrament, think is prime necessity, truth is nourishment as well as grain."
